item.title: Pakistani astronaut set to join Shenzhou XXIV mission
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07
A Pakistani astronaut is poised to take part in the coming Shenzhou XXIV spaceflight, becoming the first foreign national to fly onboard China's Tiangong space station, according to the China Manned Space Agency. In a statement released on Saturday morning, the agency said that the Pakistani astronaut will be the payload specialist in the Shenzhou XXIV mission crew and will spend several days in orbit before returning to Earth with the Shenzhou XXIII spaceship. It did not name which Pakistani astronaut will fly into space. In February 2025, the Chinese agency and Pakistan's Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission signed an agreement in Islamabad, opening bilateral cooperation to select and train Pakistani astronauts. Following rigorous screening and evaluation in three phases — preliminary selection, secondary selection, and final selection — two male Pakistani pilots were chosen as astronaut candidates: Muhammad Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud. After completing all training sessions in China and passing assessments, one of them will join a manned spaceflight mission, while the other will serve as the backup astronaut, according to the space agency. By now, the highest altitude any Pakistani has ever reached is about 87.4 km, which was reached by female polar adventurer and artist Namira Salim during a 55-minute suborbital travel arranged by American commercial space company Virgin Galactic on October 6, 2023. It is commonly recognized that the Karman line, with an altitude of 100 km above sea level, is the start of outer space and the threshold for orbital flight. Tiangong is one of the largest and most advanced structures ever deployed in Earth's orbit and is the only operating space station independently built by a single nation. In another development, the agency also published the mission emblem of the Shenzhou XXIV on Saturday.

item.title: Keep geopolitics out of marine science
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07
The politicization of marine scientific research is undermining the very cooperation needed to protect the oceans. Recently, some Philippine commentators have portrayed China's marine research activities near Huangyan Island and elsewhere in the South China Sea as potential "military threats". They have coined the term "ghost research ships", suggesting that routine scientific work is linked to military operations, submarine navigation and even anti-submarine warfare. By intertwining technological possibilities, the sensitivity of the locations and existing geopolitical tensions, they have crafted a narrative that misrepresents China's marine research as a "security concern". These claims lack supporting evidence and run counter to the international community's shared interest in advancing ocean science and protecting the marine environment. Civic leader Jose Antonio Goitia repeatedly raises doubts about the identities of the Chinese vessels, equipment and purposes without providing conclusive evidence that they are engaged in military operations. This approach turns uncertainty into a perceived certainty of "threat". Instead of proving military engagement, it relies on insinuations and possibilities that lead the public to suspect that Chinese research vessels might be conducting military operations. Since each allegation is marked as unverified or under investigation, it cannot be refuted outright, allowing the negative perceptions to persist. Official communication in the Philippines has further reinforced this narrative. Statements from the Philippine Coast Guard and military authorities have provided operational details and a broader security context, which, when combined with politically charged interpretations, blur the lines between facts and speculation. On Sept 28, the PCG linked anomalies in the Chinese research vessel Jia Hai Ke 7's automatic identification system signals to concerns about undersea communications cables and potential military data usage. Similarly, on Oct 29, a PCG spokesperson speculated without any evidence that equipment on board an unidentified vessel near Huangyan Island might be a submersible or equipment for underwater operations, although its function had yet to be established. In subsequent coverage, the PCG's ongoing investigation appeared alongside Goitia's claims that autonomous underwater vehicles were being deployed to map submarine transit routes. This presentation risks leading readers to accept the speculative claims as confirmed facts. The term "ghost research ships" itself is meant to shape public perceptions. The word "ghost" evokes a sense of secrecy, concealment and hidden intentions, associating research vessels with "military threats". This narrative blurs important distinctions among marine scientific research, hydrographic surveying, seabed mapping and military surveying. These activities may use similar technologies, but they differ significantly in purpose, methods and legal character. The mere potential of military application of equipment does not equate to military operations. If the dual-use nature of technology and the sensitivity of a location were sufficient grounds for classifying research as military activity, any country conducting seabed surveys, hydrographic measurements or ocean observations could face the same allegations. Such selective securitization lacks an objective standard and reflects the geopolitical biases in interpreting scientific activities. Marine scientific research is crucial for understanding the oceans, protecting ecosystems and addressing environmental risks that transcend national borders. Understanding ocean circulation, seabed geology, coral reef ecosystems, marine biodiversity and climate change effects requires sustained and systematic observations. Research by national institutions supports domestic marine resource management and contributes to the international body of ocean knowledge. Continuous data collection and cross-border scientific exchange are vital for coral reef conservation, marine pollution control and climate research. Marine research must comply with the rights and obligations established under international law. However, judgments about activities must be based on concrete evidence. A vessel's appearance, its technical capabilities or the potential applications of its equipment cannot establish a military purpose. The dual-use character of marine research technologies is an objective feature of modern science. Exaggerating that characteristic risks fostering mutual suspicion and creating political obstacles to marine surveys, data sharing and scientific cooperation. China's ecological surveys and conservation efforts around its Huangyan Island have clear scientific and environmental objectives. In July 2024, Chinese research institutions released a report assessing the area's environmental quality and coral reef ecosystem. In September 2025, the State Council approved the establishment of the Huangyan Dao National Nature Reserve, focusing on coral reef preservation. These initiatives reflect a commitment to using scientific investigation for ecological assessment and environmental protection. The international community has a shared interest in keeping ocean science open to cooperation. The United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development (2021-30) aims to enhance ocean observation, scientific research and knowledge sharing, providing a foundation for the sustainable use of the oceans. Against this backdrop, the securitization of marine research poses significant risks. It intensifies strategic suspicion among states, turns research vessels and data into security concerns and impedes scientific exchanges among research institutions. It also detracts from crucial environmental discussions, allowing geopolitical disputes to overshadow collective challenges such as coral reef degradation, marine pollution and climate change. The South China Sea is a shared marine environment for the region, and its ecological challenges demand sustained scientific investment and practical cooperation. Coral reef conservation, fisheries management, marine disaster monitoring and pollution control rely on reliable research and long-term observations. Countries should preserve space for scientific work, address disagreements through professional channels and foster mutual understanding through transparent, objective and verifiable information. Politicizing and militarizing research activities undermines regional stability and hinders the international community's ability to understand, protect and use the oceans sustainably. The author is a research fellow at the Institute of Peaceful Development in the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. The views don't necessarily reflect those of China Daily. If you have a specific expertise, or would like to share your thought about our stories, then send us your writings at opinion@chinadaily.com.cn, and comment@chinadaily.com.cn.

item.title: With winter here, Inner Mongolia gets to the meat of the matter
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07
Whether boiled and served by hand, roasted whole over an open fire or prepared using different cuts and cooking techniques, lamb occupies a central place in the Inner Mongolia autonomous region's culinary traditions. Nov 7 marks li dong, or Start of Winter, one of the 24 solar terms in the traditional Chinese calendar. In northern China, eating warming foods is a long-standing custom during the transition into winter. In Inner Mongolia, this seasonal tradition is closely tied to the region's pastoral food culture, where lamb has long been a staple. "Lamb is undoubtedly the most important ingredient in Inner Mongolian cuisine," says Lang Lixing, founding president of the Inner Mongolia catering and hotel industry association. Known as mengcan in Chinese, Inner Mongolian cuisine encompasses the region's diverse culinary traditions, with meat, dairy products and flour-based foods as its three main ingredient categories. Lamb occupies a central place in this culinary tradition. Inner Mongolia is one of China's major sheep-rearing regions, with annual lamb production exceeding a million metric tons, according to Lang. Its extensive grasslands, including those in Xiliin Gol League, Hulunbuir and Horqin, provide important grazing grounds. Among the region's best-known breeds is the Ujimqin sheep from Xiliin Gol League. Lang says the quality of grassland-raised lamb is closely linked to the animals' natural diet, which includes a wide variety of plants. "Good lamb should have its own distinctive flavor," Lang says. "You should be able to detect notes of milk, grass, dried fruit and wild scallions." One of the most representative ways to prepare lamb is shoubarou, or hand-grabbed lamb. Large cuts of meat are simmered in water with minimal seasoning, allowing diners to appreciate the meat's natural flavor. Once cooked, the lamb is cut into portions and eaten by hand, often accompanied by a dipping sauce. Lamb hotpot, widely enjoyed across northern China, is another popular choice during the colder months. Thinly sliced lamb is briefly swished in simmering broth before being eaten, allowing diners to enjoy its tender texture and natural flavor. Roasted whole lamb is another well-known dish, particularly suited to banquets and celebrations. A whole sheep is seasoned and slowly roasted until its skin turns golden and crisp while the meat remains tender. Other traditional preparations include blood sausages and dubaorou, in which lamb is wrapped in its own stomach lining. Traditionally, the first snowfall marked the beginning of the livestock slaughtering season for pastoral communities, as the cold weather provided natural conditions for preserving meat. The period also marked a time to celebrate the year's harvest, with families preparing various lamb dishes to share. For those enjoying lamb during the colder months, a balanced diet is also important. Nutritionist Xing Yanchun recommends pairing lamb with vegetables such as winter melon, cabbage and mushrooms, as well as potatoes and sweet potatoes. These vegetables provide dietary variety and complement the richness of lamb. Inner Mongolian lamb cuisine extends well beyond its familiar traditional dishes. Lang has helped develop a standardized whole-lamb banquet. The latest version features 20 dishes made with 21 different cuts and edible parts of the lamb, including the head, tongue, liver, ribs, stomach and tail.

item.title: China, Gabon elevate bilateral ties
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07
China and Gabon upgraded bilateral relations to a community with a shared future for the new era on Friday as part of their efforts to enhance traditional friendship and pragmatic cooperation. President Xi Jinping and Gabonese President Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema announced the elevation of the two countries' ties during their talks at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. Nguema started his five-day state visit to China on Tuesday, his first since taking office in May 2025. He recently visited Shanghai, where he attended the ongoing ninth China International Import Expo. During their talks, Xi hailed the long-standing traditional friendship between China and Gabon, noting that the two countries treat each other as equals and support each other for shared development. The China-Gabon relationship has withstood the test of a changing international landscape and remains rock-solid as ever, he said, adding that deepening the two countries' ties aligns with the common aspirations of both peoples and the broader trend of unity and self-strengthening among Global South countries. Xi expressed China's willingness to be a reliable friend and partner of Gabon in its independent development, support its autonomy in politics, economy and diplomacy, and work together to build a China-Gabon community with a shared future for the new era. Noting that mutual support is a distinctive feature and political advantage of China-Gabon relations, Xi emphasized that China will continue to support Gabon in exploring a development path suited to its national conditions. China is ready to engage in close exchanges at all levels with Gabon, share experiences in party and state governance, and support it in enhancing its governance capacity, he said. The two nations enjoy economic complementarity and have a great potential for cooperation, Xi said, calling on China and Gabon to strengthen the alignment of their development strategies and cultivate new growth drivers for collaboration. He encouraged the Central African country to take advantage of China's zero-tariff treatment, as well as its "green channel" policy to fast-track customs clearance for African agricultural products, in order to promote Gabon's industrial development, job creation and livelihood improvement and enhance its capacity for independent economic growth. In May, China granted zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with which it has diplomatic relations. Xi noted that his vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, along with the four major global initiatives he proposed, serves the common interests of the Global South and African countries. China supports Gabon in playing a greater role in international and regional affairs, and is willing to strengthen exchanges and cooperation with it to build a better world together, he added. Nguema said the friendship between Gabon and China has spanned more than half a century, with strategic mutual trust always being the cornerstone of their partnership. Cooperation between the two countries is vibrant, significantly promoting Gabon's economic diversification and improving the livelihood of its people in areas such as infrastructure, energy, healthcare, education and vocational training, he said. Nguema emphasized that Gabon firmly adheres to the one-China principle. He congratulated the Communist Party of China on successfully holding the fifth plenary session of its 20th Central Committee, and said that Gabon looks forward to promoting party-to-party exchanges and learning from China's successful experiences in party and state governance. Gabon is willing to further deepen pragmatic cooperation with China and welcomes more Chinese investment to aid its industrialization and sustainable development, he said. Nguema described China-Africa cooperation as mutually beneficial and win-win, saying that the zero-tariff treatment meets the needs of African countries, allows more African products to enter China's vast market, and holds historic significance for Africa's development. Gabon highly appreciates China's advocacy of multilateralism and its fair and just stance in international and regional affairs, Nguema said, adding that his country is willing to closely coordinate with China to strengthen Africa-China solidarity and cooperation and jointly safeguard the interests of Global South nations. After the talks, the two heads of state witnessed the signing of multiple cooperation documents in areas such as the Global Security Initiative, zero-tariff treatment, industrial and supply chains, and Chinese language education. The two countries issued a joint statement on the building of a China-Gabon community with a shared future for the new era. On Friday, Nguema also held separate meetings in Beijing with Premier Li Qiang and Zhao Leji, chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, China's top legislature.

item.title: Governing the ocean, shaping our future
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07
The ocean is central to our shared future, but it is also a place where competition, tensions and environmental challenges are on the rise. At the 7th Symposium on Global Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance, more than 400 participants from over 30 countries and regions—policymakers, representatives of international organizations, scholars and industry representatives—are focusing on some of the most pressing ocean issues of our time. The symposium, running Friday to Sunday, is jointly organized by institutions including the Huayang Center for Maritime Cooperation and Ocean Governance and the China Ocean Development Foundation.

item.title: Young Australians urged to forge bonds
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07
President Xi Jinping has encouraged young Australians to continue promoting the friendship between China and Australia and carry it forward from generation to generation. He made the remarks in a recent reply to a letter from 110 Australian students. In his letter dated Oct 28, Xi said he was pleased to learn that the students had recently visited China for the Sino-Australian Collegiate Rowing and Dragon Boat Friendship Challenge, where they competed alongside Chinese university students, held in-depth exchanges, forged friendships across borders and created lasting memories together. China and Australia share a longstanding tradition of friendly exchanges, Xi said, adding that the future of bilateral relations lies with the younger generation. He expressed hope that the students would continue to promote China-Australia friendship, serve as torchbearers of bilateral friendship and cooperation, and pass the baton of friendship to future generations. In September, 110 students from the University of Sydney and other Australian universities jointly wrote to Xi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to share their experiences of visiting China. They expressed their admiration for China's long history, rich culture and capacity for scientific and technological innovation, as well as showed their eagerness to carry forward the bilateral friendship and deepen mutual understanding. During their visit to China from Sept 8 to 15, the Australian students traveled to Nanjing, Yangzhou, Changzhou and Zhenjiang in Jiangsu province. They participated in exchanges with Chinese students, experienced China's intangible cultural heritage, and visited university robotics institutes and new energy companies. "Our time in Nanjing has given us the opportunity to experience the energy of a modern Chinese city while learning about her history, traditions and people," the students wrote in the letter. "We have been welcomed warmly and have gained a greater appreciation for the importance of hard work, commitment and teamwork — values that we share through sport." Chinese Ambassador to Australia Liu Jinsong, who delivered Xi's letter to student representatives on Friday at a ceremony held in Adelaide, Australia, described his reply as "warm and heartfelt, and rich in significance". Daniel Wiersema, a finance and engineering student at Adelaide University, told China Daily that they wrote the letter because they were deeply moved by the generosity of the Chinese people during their visit, and they felt they needed to express their gratitude to President Xi for such an experience. Wiersema said the trip granted them the opportunity to participate in a dragon boat race for the first time, and teaming up with Chinese students allowed them to build lifelong friendships and learn more about student life in China. He noted that youth exchanges were important for strengthening bilateral relations, because "the youth is the future of both of our nations". He added that friendships formed between young people could help foster a lasting relationship between Australia and China. The visit also offered Anja Felderhof, a rower with the Adelaide University Boat Club, a fresh perspective on China. Felderhof, who is studying mechanical engineering at the university, told China Daily that despite language barriers, the warmth and kindness of local people left a deep impression on her. The trip "opened my eyes to a country I wouldn't have thought I'd experience", the student said, adding that she would definitely like to visit China again. Tom Steer, deputy vice-chancellor for student experience and success at Adelaide University, said at Friday's ceremony that the two-way exchange has built "understanding, lasting friendships and connections" between the two nations, and has brought together "learning, culture and the shared experiences of young people". The September event was part of the China-Australia Program for Youth Exchange, which aims to bring 3,000 to 5,000 young Australians to China for exchanges and study tours for three years, starting from 2025.

item.title: Giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang make public debut in Atlanta
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07
Mark Fisher, a captain at FedEx, was one of the pilots flying giant pandas Ping Ping and Fu Shuang to Atlanta from Chengdu in September. Fisher said it took about 16 hours to fly the pandas over. "It was a long trip, and they were very well taken care of on the airplane. Now to see them in their new enclosure is very exciting for us," he said with his wife by his side, adding that as a native Atlantan, bringing the pandas here has been a great honor. The new Atlanta home of the giant pandas, Arthur M. Blank Panda Grove, opened on Friday. Long awaited after their arrival in late September, this debut offers the first public view of the pair. "Everybody's been talking about it locally, everybody's excited and [has] been waiting patiently for this day," Fisher told China Daily on Friday. Chinese Ambassador Xie Feng and Zoo Atlanta President and CEO Raymond King cut the ribbon for the $6 million updated Arthur M Blank Panda Grove on Friday. Photo provided to chinadaily.com.cn Indeed, a long line began to form in front of Zoo Atlanta about an hour before its door opened at 10:30 am. Many of them were eager to get the first glimpse of the new residents from China after quarantining for about a month. The first pair - Lun Lun and Yang Yang - had lived here from 1999 to 2024, producing seven cubs in total with a one hundred percent survival rate. "I think today is a great reunion for us," Raymond King, president and CEO at Zoo Atlanta, told China Daily during the ribbon-cutting ceremony shortly before the door opened to the public. "We've missed our pandas for two years, and the citizens of Atlanta have certainly missed them." King said that people come to see the pandas and often leave with a deeper appreciation for conservation as well as Chinese culture. "The relationships that have been established in that mutual partnership of conservation go a long way to bridge the differences that people perceive exist between the two cultures, and find that at the end of the day, while the governments may disagree at different times, the peoples want the same thing," King said. "We all have shared value in family and friendships and preserving our environment. It breaks down a lot of the barriers that would otherwise exist." A family from California enjoys a selfie with giant panda Fu Shuang at Zoo Atlanta on Friday. Photo by May Zhou / China Daily Chinese Ambassador to the US Xie Feng, addressing guests at the ceremony, said that the arrival of the new pair of pandas is "a vivid testament to the practical sub-national cooperation between China and the United States" and "instill fresh vitality into practical cooperation between China and Georgia, including the city of Atlanta, and will usher in a new phase in China-US sub-national engagement." Ping Ping and Fu Shuang arrived three days after President Xi Jinping announced during his September state visit that the pandas would reach Atlanta within days. Xie recounted Zoo Atlanta's history of panda conservation: in 1999, giant pandas Lun Lun and Yang Yang became the first panda residents at Zoo Atlanta. Under the meticulous care of the team here, they gave birth to a total of seven cubs across five litters in 25 years, including two pairs of twins, creating the most successful breeding record in China-US giant panda cooperation. New resident Ping Ping is a natural continuation of that family lineage, Xie said, as Yang Yang is his uncle — his mother's elder brother. Fu Shuang's lineage is famous. "Her father is no one else but the real-world inspiration behind Po, the main character of Kung Fu Panda 2," Xie said. Fu Shuang enjoys bamboo at Zoo Atlanta on the opening day on Friday. Photo by May Zhou / China Daily Xie pointed to Atlanta residents' pride when bamboo from their properties was selected to feed the pandas. He also said the FedEx Panda Express carrying Ping Ping and Fu Shuang was the most tracked international flight in the world. "The arrival of the new pair of pandas is China's sincere response to the aspirations of the American people," Xie said. "Love for pandas is everywhere we turn." Xie said panda conservation success in the US contributed to "a joint China-US solution to global biodiversity protection" and serves "as a compelling example of how China and the United States working together can get a lot of big and great things done". Sonny Perdue, a former Georgia governor, veterinarian and chancellor of the University System of Georgia, recalled helping examine Mei Lan, Zoo Atlanta's first panda cub, in December 2006, when the cub was nearly four months old. "I got to weigh and measure the little cub, who was fourteen pounds at that point," Perdue said. "So I'm glad that my degree as a veterinarian came in handy during that effort as governor." He said Atlanta was proud to be home to one of only three US zoos with giant pandas and to participate in international conservation partnerships that promote goodwill. King welcomed delegates from the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding, the China Wildlife Conservation Association, the Chinese Embassy as well as supporters and partners for the panda conservation programs from Atlanta. "This extraordinary spirit of partnership helps create a future for a species that is truly beloved the world over," King said. "For some, a visit to the Arthur and Blank Panda Grove will become a cherished family memory. For others, it may spark a lifelong interest in wildlife, a commitment to conservation, or even a future career caring for animals." The Chinese Embassy provided an all-day cultural experience for enthusiastic panda visitors on the opening day, many of whom came from out of the state. Panda visitors enjoyed gifts such as panda toys, stickers, post cards, and headbands. Some tried their hands on Chinese calligraphy and making book markers. mayzhou@chinadaiyusa.com

item.title: President: Nation can help Europe tackle its problems
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-07
President Xi Jinping said on Friday that a growing and developing China is not a source of Europe's problems, but a partner and fellow traveler that can help Europe address its challenges. He made the remarks when meeting with Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker in Beijing. China and Europe should resolve trade and economic frictions through dialogue and negotiation to achieve win-win outcomes and common development, Xi said. Noting that this year marks the 55th anniversary of diplomatic relations between China and Austria, he said the two countries have upheld mutual respect, openness, inclusiveness and mutually beneficial cooperation, steadily strengthening political trust and delivering tangible benefits to their peoples. Trust and friendship are valuable qualities of China-Austria relations, transcending differences in social systems, history, culture and stages of development, he said. Xi called on both sides to consolidate political trust, sustain the positive momentum of high-level exchanges, and build trust and dispel doubts through communication, laying a solid political foundation for future cooperation. He said that during the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period, China will continue to foster emerging industries, upgrade traditional industries and expand opening-up, with a focus on the services sector. "China Opportunity 2.0" will bring benefits from both the country's market and its innovation, he added. Xi said that China is ready to expand practical cooperation with Austria in emerging fields, including new energy vehicles, artificial intelligence, the digital economy and green development, creating new engines of growth in economic and trade ties. He also called for broader people-to-people exchanges and easier travel to bring the two peoples closer together. Noting the turbulence in the international landscape and the headwinds of unilateralism and protectionism, Xi said the two countries should practice true multilateralism, support free trade and contribute to a more just and equitable global governance system. Stocker reaffirmed Austria's commitment to the one-China policy, and its willingness to strengthen cooperation with China in trade, investment, science, technology and innovation, while promoting cultural, tourism and people-to-people exchanges. He expressed Austria's support for the development of Europe-China relations and its hope that both sides would resolve economic and trade differences through candid dialogue and consultation. Austria is ready to strengthen multilateral coordination with China to promote sustainable development, tackle climate change and other challenges, and safeguard global prosperity and stability, he said. On Friday, Premier Li Qiang held a welcome ceremony for Stocker. During their talks, Li said that China is ready to import more high-quality Austrian goods and expand cooperation in areas such as advanced manufacturing to deliver more tangible results. China supports more Chinese companies investing in Austria and hopes that Austria will provide them with a fair, equitable and nondiscriminatory business environment, Li said. The two leaders also witnessed the signing of several cooperation documents in areas including economic and trade cooperation and social security. The Austrian chancellor is due to conclude his six-day official visit on Saturday. This is his first visit to China since taking office in March last year, and the first by an Austrian chancellor in seven years. He began the trip in Shanghai, where he attended the ninth China International Import Expo. In social media posts during the visit, Stocker said the world needed dialogue and reliable partnerships amid turmoil, and that his trip aimed to secure jobs and opportunities for Austrian businesses. Statistics show the value of bilateral trade reached $12.5 billion in 2025, up 2 percent year-on-year. According to the Austria Press Agency, around 650 Austrian companies run some 900 operations in China, with machinery and equipment among Austria's main exports to the country. Cui Hongjian, director of Beijing Foreign Studies University's Center for European Union and Regional Development Studies, said that visits to China by several European leaders in the past two months show that shared economic interests and Europe's need for dialogue and cooperation with China remain strong despite differences. Pragmatic engagement could help Europe better understand China's policies, identify cooperation opportunities and prevent disagreements from escalating, Cui said, adding that the two sides could find pragmatic solutions to their differences if they moved beyond political obstacles and unhelpful narratives.
